desc:
Rearrange nums so that non-negative and negative values alternate, starting with a non-negative value. Non-negative values keep their relative order among themselves and negative values keep theirs. When one kind runs out, all remaining values of the other kind are appended at the end in their original order. Return the rearranged array.

nums = [3, -1, -2, 5, 4, -7, -8, -9]
result = [3, -1, 5, -2, 4, -7, -8, -9]
nums = [-4, -5, 0]
result = [0, -4, -5]

Zero counts as non-negative.
hints: Sorting by sign does not alternate the values. Think of the answer as built by drawing alternately from two queues: one of the non-negative values, one of the negative values.
Use two read pointers, p over the next non-negative value and q over the next negative value, both advancing through nums from the left.

While both kinds are still available, output one non-negative then one negative (move p and q to the next element of their kind). Afterwards output all remaining elements of whichever kind is left, in order.
editorial: The answer is a merge of two subsequences, the non-negative one and the negative one, taken one element at a time starting with a non-negative. When one subsequence is exhausted the other is simply appended, which is exactly what the statement asks.

Implementing it with two pointers avoids building the lists: p and q are the indices of the next unused non-negative and negative value; after taking one, advance the pointer to the next element of the same sign. Each pointer only moves forward, so the total number of steps is at most 2n.

Time O(n); the output array is the only extra memory, O(n). Doing this in O(1) extra space while preserving order is a famous hard exercise (it needs rotations), which is why this version returns a new array.
